name: Chin and jaw exercise routines

lead: Chin and jaw exercise routines are workouts for the chewing muscles, such as chewing hard gum or using a jaw trainer, intended to build the masseters and sharpen the jawline. Enthusiasts also pair them with mewing and neck training.
The masseter is a muscle of mastication that can enlarge with habits such as gum chewing or clenching, which is the basis for the idea.

paras: People chew tough gum or use a resistance device on the molars, some adding tongue posture and neck work. Forum users report short-term facial puffiness after sessions.
Forum posters mention TMJ discomfort and overdeveloped temporalis; the masseter can also enlarge unevenly, and jaw exercise research in medicine is aimed at TMD treatment rather than appearance.

angle.text: Users train the masseters hoping for a squarer, firmer jawline. Muscle bulk at the angle of the jaw is the mechanism they cite.

lead: Chin and jaw exercise routines are training habits for the muscles of the lower face, intended to build the masseters and define the jawline. Looksmaxxing forum users describe chewing, resistance devices and tongue posture work as part of routines.[1][2]

The masseter is a muscle of mastication, and Wikipedia notes its enlargement is linked to habitual clenching, grinding or constant gum chewing.[3] Medical research on jaw exercises centres on temporomandibular disorders (TMD), including randomised trials comparing counselling with counselling plus jaw exercises and comparing exercises with splint therapy.[4][5]

paras: Routines include chewing tough gum, resistance trainers and tongue posture practice, discussed alongside neck training.[1]

A looksmax.org user reported more defined masseters with a trainer but a large pumped temporalis, and others in the thread warned of TMJ risk.[1] Another asked whether post-exercise facial bloating was normal, and replies disagreed about whether chewing builds a better jawline.[2] A third thread asked about a YouTuber's routine and received sceptical answers.[6]

Masseter hypertrophy can occur with bruxism or constant gum chewing and can cause asymmetry.[3] Clinical research focuses on TMD: a 2023 randomised trial compared counselling with counselling plus jaw exercises for disc displacement with reduction,[4] a 1999 trial compared jaw exercises with occlusal splints,[5] and a 2010 review synthesised systematic reviews on TMD management.[7]
Trials of jaw exercises address pain and function in TMD rather than appearance.[4][5] No studies found testing jaw exercises for jawline definition.

lore.intro: Jaw exercise threads on looksmax.org discuss devices, chewing gum and side effects.[1][2][6]
